Q001024:
Why this is correct:
VPC peering is non-transitive: A can't reach C through B, even with routes. A direct A-C peering or a Transit Gateway (hub-and-spoke routing) is required.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups in C: the traffic never arrives, since peering doesn't forward.
• Overlapping CIDRs: not the stated problem; routes were correct.
• Different Organizations: peering works across accounts and organizations.

Key takeaway: peering is one-to-one; for transitive routing, use Transit Gateway.
Q001025:
Why this is correct:
99.99% requires no single point of failure at the location level: two connections at two different Direct Connect locations, each with its own device, give automatic BGP failover if a location fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One DX + VPN: VPN backup has variable performance and falls short of the 99.99% design.
• Two connections at one location: a location failure takes both down.
• VPN only: internet-dependent and not suitable for this SLA.

Key takeaway: high resiliency = separate DX locations.
Q001026:
Why this is correct:
A Transit Gateway gives hub-and-spoke routing for all 40 VPCs, and a Direct Connect gateway with a transit VIF connects that hub to on-premises over the shared DX link.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full mesh peering: 780 connections, and peering can't share DX transitively.
• VPN between every pair: unmanageable.
• One giant VPC: loses account and blast-radius separation.

Key takeaway: many VPCs + on-prem → TGW + DX gateway.
Q001027:
Why this is correct:
Resolver inbound endpoints let on-premises DNS forward queries into the VPC (for private zones), and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules send VPC queries for on-premises domains to on-premises DNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: covers one direction.
• EC2 forwarders replacing Resolver: extra servers to run, and unnecessary.
• Public hosted zone: exposes internal names.

Key takeaway: inbound = on-prem → AWS; outbound = AWS → on-prem.
Q001028:
Why this is correct:
S3 supports gateway endpoints (route table entries, no cost). Third-party SaaS APIs are reached privately through PrivateLink interface endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway for SaaS: gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.
• Interface for both: works for S3 but costs more; the key point is SaaS needs PrivateLink.
• Reversed: SaaS can't use gateway endpoints.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB → gateway endpoints; everything else → interface endpoints.
Q001029:
Why this is correct:
VPC IPAM plans, allocates, and tracks non-overlapping CIDRs across accounts and Regions from managed pools, preventing conflicts as 200 VPCs are created.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Teams choose independently: overlaps will block future connectivity; IAM doesn't prevent overlap.
• Same /16 everywhere: can't interconnect.
• Public IP ranges: waste scarce addresses and don't fit private networks.

Key takeaway: org-wide IP planning → VPC IPAM.
Q001030:
Why this is correct:
Maximum resiliency uses separate connections on separate devices at two locations (four connections), surviving a device, connection, or location failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two connections on the same device: device or location failure breaks both.
• Dedicated + hosted at one location: location failure breaks both.
• DX + VPN in the same location's path: not the maximum resiliency model.

Key takeaway: survive any single failure → maximum resiliency (2 locations × 2 devices).
Q001031:
Why this is correct:
Separate TGW route tables: spoke attachments associate with a table that only has routes to shared services, and the shared services table has routes to all spokes. Spokes can't reach each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One table with propagation: every spoke can reach every other spoke.
• Peering: loses central control and doesn't scale.
• NACLs per spoke: brittle and hard to manage.

Key takeaway: segment with TGW route table association and propagation.
Q001032:
Why this is correct:
VPC Flow Logs on the ENIs record accepted and rejected flows with timestamps, showing whether traffic was blocked during the failure windows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: application traces, not network accept/reject decisions.
• Inspector reachability: static analysis, not what happened at specific times.
• Config history: shows rule changes but not traffic outcomes.

Key takeaway: what actually happened to traffic → Flow Logs.
Q001033:
Why this is correct:
A PrivateLink endpoint service behind an NLB exposes only the API. Customers create interface endpoints in their VPCs, with no CIDR coordination or full network access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: exposes whole networks and needs non-overlapping CIDRs.
• TGW shared to customers: gives broad network connectivity.
• Public ALB with WAF allow lists: internet exposure.

Key takeaway: expose one service to many VPCs → PrivateLink.
Q001035:
Why this is correct:
A Direct Connect gateway can associate with Transit Gateways in multiple Regions through a transit VIF, giving on-premises access to all Regions over the DX connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW peering via one Region: extra hops and complexity.
• Public VIF: reaches public endpoints, not VPCs.
• Separate VPNs: doesn't use Direct Connect.

Key takeaway: one DX, many Regions → DX gateway + TGWs.
Q001036:
Why this is correct:
Overlapping CIDRs can't be routed directly. NAT (for example, a NAT or proxy layer with the TGW) translates only the specific endpoints that must talk, until re-IP is possible. PrivateLink is another option for specific services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering with the same CIDR: not allowed.
• Routing 10.0.0.0/16 to the other VPC: conflicts with local routes.
• TGW propagation: overlapping routes can't be resolved.

Key takeaway: overlapping CIDRs → translate (NAT) or expose services (PrivateLink).
Q001037:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on and assigns permission sets to groups for specific accounts, which creates scoped roles in each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito: for application users, not workforce AWS access.
• Replicated IAM users: long-term credentials and sprawl.
• Manual cross-account roles: inconsistent and hard to audit.

Key takeaway: workforce access across accounts → Identity Center.
Q001039:
Why this is correct:
KMS multi-Region keys share key material and ID across Regions, so data encrypted in one Region can be decrypted in another, which fits Global Tables with customer managed keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS managed keys: not customer managed.
• Independent keys with the same alias: different key material, so cross-Region decryption fails.
• Client-side encryption with a shared secret: complex and weaker key management.

Key takeaway: cross-Region encrypt/decrypt with one logical key → multi-Region keys.
Q001041:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless. Allowing inbound 443 isn't enough; outbound rules must allow ephemeral ports (1024-65535) for responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IGW route for a private subnet: not the issue and would make it public.
• EBS encryption: unrelated to network traffic.
• Security group return rules: SGs are stateful.

Key takeaway: NACL changes → check both directions.
Q001042:
Why this is correct:
A cross-account bucket policy grants the partner, SSE-KMS with a key whose policy grants both accounts controls encryption, an aws:SecureTransport condition enforces TLS, and CloudTrail records access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SFTP with shared static credentials: weak identity.
• Replication with default encryption: loses key control.
• Public bucket with presigned URLs: violates the requirement.

Key takeaway: cross-account sensitive sharing = bucket policy + KMS key policy + TLS + audit.
Q001043:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates servers at block level to AWS, giving an RPO of seconds and failover within minutes, with non-disruptive drills.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Backup: periodic backups, not continuous replication.
• MGN one-time migration: for migrations, not ongoing DR.
• DataSync: file transfers, not server replication.

Key takeaway: server DR to AWS → Elastic Disaster Recovery.
Q001044:
Why this is correct:
AWS Backup copies to another account and Region, with Vault Lock in compliance mode, retain backups for 7 years and prevent deletion by anyone, including administrators.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 lifecycle without Object Lock: deletable.
• 35-day automated backups: too short.
• Cron script copies: fragile and deletable.

Key takeaway: long retention + immutable + cross-account → AWS Backup + Vault Lock.
Q001045:
Why this is correct:
Horizontal scaling across AZs with an Auto Scaling group adds instances as demand grows, handling sustained 5x load without the single-instance ceiling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent copies: pays for peak capacity all year.
• Pre-sale vertical scaling: ceilings and downtime.
• Larger single instance: still a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: elastic scale-out beats bigger boxes.
Q001046:
Why this is correct:
The standby scales slowly because scaling isn't prepared. Pre-configuring aggressive scaling triggered by failover automation, and testing it, meets the RTO.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Relaxing RPO: doesn't help recovery time.
• Pilot light: even less standby capacity, so slower.
• Active-active: meets the goal but at much higher cost than needed.

Key takeaway: warm standby works only if scale-up is automated and tested.
Q001047:
Why this is correct:
Pilot light keeps only data running, so the app tier must be built quickly. Prebuilt AMIs or IaC and automated, tested runbooks make that rebuild fast and reliable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Relaxing RPO: RPO isn't the problem.
• Snapshots instead of replication: worsens RPO.
• Backups only: slower than pilot light.

Key takeaway: pilot light depends on automation for the missing tiers.
Q001048:
Why this is correct:
Near-zero RTO and RPO with both Regions serving traffic is multi-site active-active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Backup and restore: hours of recovery.
• Pilot light: minutes to hours to build capacity.
• Warm standby: faster, but not simultaneous full serving.

Key takeaway: near-zero RTO/RPO → active-active.
Q001049:
Why this is correct:
Predictive scaling learns the daily pattern and adds capacity ahead of the 9 AM peak, and target tracking handles unexpected spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled only: misses unplanned spikes.
• Simple scaling: slower and coarser.
• Manual scaling: unreliable.

Key takeaway: known patterns → predictive; surprises → target tracking.
Q001050:
Why this is correct:
Failover routing with a health check on the primary answers with the secondary record automatically when the primary is unhealthy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing with a runbook: manual.
• 50/50 weighted: sends traffic to the standby all the time.
• Manual CNAME: slow.

Key takeaway: automatic DNS DR → failover records + health checks.
Q001051:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Global Database replicates to secondary Regions with typically sub-second lag and supports fast promotion, meeting an RPO of seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Binlog replicas plus snapshots: higher lag and slower recovery.
• Daily manual copies: RPO of a day.
• Serverless auto-pause: not a DR mechanism.

Key takeaway: cross-Region Aurora DR → Global Database.
Q001052:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates blocks continuously (RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes), while snapshot-based backup and restore has larger RPO and slower recovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Re-architecture required: DRS works with existing servers.
• Free automatic drills with backups: not true.
• DRS always cheaper: it adds continuous replication costs.

Key takeaway: continuous replication vs. periodic snapshots.
Q001053:
Why this is correct:
If the cooldown or instance warm-up is too short, the policy reacts before new instances contribute, causing repeated scale-out and scale-in (flapping).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Zero grace period: causes health replacements, not scaling flaps.
• Too few subnets: causes launch failures, not flapping.
• No launch template: the group couldn't launch at all.

Key takeaway: flapping → tune warm-up and cooldown.
Q001054:
Why this is correct:
Separate Production and Non-Production OUs let different SCPs apply to each environment, with dedicated accounts per workload.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tags only: can be changed by users and are weaker guardrails.
• No OU structure: can't apply policies at scale.
• One OU with IAM: IAM isn't an org-wide guardrail.

Key takeaway: environment guardrails → OUs + SCPs.
Q001055:
Why this is correct:
A GuardDuty delegated administrator aggregates member findings, and EventBridge rules in the administrator account route them to a central bus or targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Polling Lambdas: complex and fragile.
• Daily CSV: not near real time.
• CloudTrail Insights: not GuardDuty findings.

Key takeaway: org-wide security findings → delegated admin + EventBridge.
Q001056:
Why this is correct:
VPC sharing through RAM lets participant accounts launch resources into the owner's subnets, while the network team keeps control of the VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreating VPCs: defeats central management.
• Roles into the network account: resources belong to the wrong account.
• Peering: separate VPCs, not shared subnets.

Key takeaway: central subnets for many accounts → RAM subnet sharing.
Q001057:
Why this is correct:
SCPs set the maximum available permissions for accounts in an OU. If an SCP doesn't allow (or explicitly denies) s3:DeleteBucket, no IAM policy can grant it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Matching allow in the SCP: only if the org chooses to permit it; the developer can't fix it.
• Only direct children: SCPs apply through the OU hierarchy.
• IAM overrides SCPs: the opposite.

Key takeaway: effective permissions = IAM ∩ SCP.
Q001059:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail delivers all accounts' events to a central Log Archive bucket, where Athena or CloudTrail Lake can query them without per-account setup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: network traffic, not API events.
• On-prem SIEM without aggregation: fragmented.
• Per-account trails: inconsistent and complex.

Key takeaway: org-wide API audit → organization trail.
Q001060:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower provides prebuilt baselines, controls, and Account Factory quickly, but with less flexibility than a fully custom landing zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom always cheaper: not generally true, and it costs engineering time.
• Replaces Organizations: it's built on Organizations.
• Supports every custom need: it has limits.

Key takeaway: Control Tower trades flexibility for speed and standardization.
Q001061:
Why this is correct:
Sharing the TGW through RAM lets spoke accounts create their own attachments without being given any permissions in the network account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: loses the hub.
• IAM users in the network account: over-privileged and long-term credentials.
• Network team creates each attachment: slow and centralizes work.

Key takeaway: shared network resources → RAM.
Q001062:
Why this is correct:
Centralized governance gives consistency and simpler audits but can slow teams. Decentralized gives agility but risks inconsistency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No tradeoff: there is one.
• Removes SCPs: SCPs are central tools.
• Decentralized always cheaper: not guaranteed.

Key takeaway: governance is a tradeoff between control and autonomy.
Q001063:
Why this is correct:
SCPs apply to all accounts in an OU. If resources still appear in unapproved Regions, the SCP logic is likely wrong: a bad aws:RequestedRegion condition, an allow that overrides nothing, or missing exemptions for global services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't enforce Regions with SCPs: they can.
• Must be in the management OU: the opposite; SCPs don't apply to the management account.
• Manual re-registration: not required.

Key takeaway: debug the SCP's conditions and structure.
Q001065:
Why this is correct:
Interruptible, checkpointed batch work gets the lowest cost from Spot Instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-Demand: full price.
• Dedicated Hosts: expensive and for licensing or compliance.
• 3-year RIs: commit to capacity used only at night.

Key takeaway: interruptible + checkpointed → Spot.
Q001068:
Why this is correct:
Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization history with machine learning and recommends specific instance types and EBS configurations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: broad checks, fewer specific rightsizing recommendations.
• Storage Lens: S3.
• Budgets: spend alerts.

Key takeaway: ML rightsizing → Compute Optimizer.
Q001070:
Why this is correct:
Enforced cost allocation tags attribute direct costs, and Cost Categories can split shared costs (such as TGW or NAT charges) across business units by rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Spreadsheets: manual and error-prone.
• Group by service only: no business-unit view.
• Account-level only: shared accounts serve many units.

Key takeaway: shared cost allocation → tags + Cost Categories.
Q001072:
Why this is correct:
Standard RIs give slightly larger discounts but are tied to instance family and Region. Compute Savings Plans apply across families, Regions, Fargate, and Lambda, which suits variable usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cancel anytime: both are commitments.
• Identical: they differ in flexibility.
• RIs cover Fargate and Lambda: they don't.

Key takeaway: variable usage → Compute Savings Plans.
Q001073:
Why this is correct:
Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to spot unusual spend, identifies the service or account, and sends alerts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: optimization tips.
• Fixed billing alarm: doesn't identify the cause.
• Manual review: slow.

Key takeaway: unexpected spend → Cost Anomaly Detection.
Q001074:
Why this is correct:
Consolidated billing combines usage for volume tiers and, unless disabled, shares RI and Savings Plans discounts across accounts. Subsidiaries can see their own costs, and sharing can be turned off per account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabled by default: sharing is on by default.
• Each account must buy its own: not required.
• Only the management account benefits: discounts are shared.

Key takeaway: consolidated billing shares discounts by default.
Q001075:
Why this is correct:
Handling the 2-minute interruption notice (checkpoint and drain), diversifying instance types and AZs, and using a capacity-optimized allocation strategy reduce interruptions and their impact.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All On-Demand: gives up the savings.
• Disable notices: loses the warning.
• Higher max price: Spot interruptions aren't driven by your bid.

Key takeaway: design for Spot: diversify and handle notices.
Q001076:
Why this is correct:
Regional RIs apply to usage in any AZ in the Region and across sizes in the family (size flexibility), fitting a workload that moved across AZs. Zonal RIs can be modified to Regional.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't modify: RIs can be modified (and Standard RIs sold).
• Cancel for On-Demand: RIs can't be canceled.
• More Zonal RIs: over-commits.

Key takeaway: flexibility across AZs → Regional RIs.
Q001077:
Why this is correct:
Service-managed StackSets deploy to target OUs and automatically to new accounts added to them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config remediation: fixes drift, not full baselines.
• Manual stacks: don't scale.
• Custom Lambda on account creation: reinvents StackSets.

Key takeaway: org-wide baselines → StackSets with auto-deployment.
Q001078:
Why this is correct:
The pipeline assumes a narrowly scoped cross-account role in production that can only pass a CloudFormation service role, which CloudFormation uses to create resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: over-privileged.
• Root credentials: never.
• Pipeline in production: couples tooling with production.

Key takeaway: cross-account deployments via scoped roles.
Q001079:
Why this is correct:
Amazon MSK runs Apache Kafka as a managed service, removing broker patching and failure handling while keeping Kafka APIs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ASG around self-managed Kafka: still self-managed.
• Kinesis: requires rewriting producers and consumers.
• SQS: different semantics.

Key takeaway: managed Kafka → MSK.
Q001080:
Why this is correct:
A Lambda-backed custom resource runs your code during stack create, update, and delete to manage resources CloudFormation doesn't support natively.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Macro: transforms templates; doesn't call external APIs at deploy time.
• Config remediation: not provisioning.
• Manual SSM document: outside the stack lifecycle.

Key takeaway: unsupported resources → custom resources.
Q001081:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild caching (S3 or local) keeps dependencies between builds, avoiding reinstalling everything each time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Persistent EC2 build server: more operations.
• More parallel stages: doesn't speed dependency installation.
• Bigger compute: faster but still reinstalls.

Key takeaway: repeated dependency installs → caching.
Q001083:
Why this is correct:
ContinueUpdateRollback resumes the rollback and can skip resources that can't be rolled back, returning the stack to a usable state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Editing states in the console: not possible.
• Automatic retry: doesn't happen.
• Delete and recreate: destructive.

Key takeaway: stuck rollback → ContinueUpdateRollback.
Q001084:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS creates a replacement task set, shifts traffic gradually (linear or canary), and rolls back on CloudWatch alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• New cluster with manual DNS: slow and manual.
• Manual desired count: no traffic shifting.
• Rolling update without alarms: no automatic rollback.

Key takeaway: gradual ECS releases with rollback → CodeDeploy blue/green.
Q001085:
Why this is correct:
Service Catalog offers approved CloudFormation products that developers can launch themselves, using a launch constraint role instead of broad permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public SSM documents: not governed products.
• CreateStack permissions: developers can deploy anything.
• Tickets: not self-service.

Key takeaway: governed self-service → Service Catalog.
Q001086:
Why this is correct:
Systems Manager covers hybrid fleets: Patch Manager for patching, Inventory for software data, and Run Command for commands.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config remediation: compliance, not fleet management.
• Drift detection: for stacks, not servers.
• Cron jobs: unmanaged and inconsistent.

Key takeaway: hybrid fleet operations → Systems Manager.
Q001087:
Why this is correct:
Losing 45 minutes of data means asynchronous replication lag exceeded the RPO. Tighter replication (such as Aurora Global Database with lag monitoring) reduces data loss.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Slow scaling: affects RTO, not lost data.
• RTO misconfigured: RTO isn't about data loss.
• Health check interval: affects failover timing, not replication lag.
• Log bucket CRR: unrelated to database data loss.

Key takeaway: data loss = RPO problem = replication lag.
Q001088:
Why this is correct:
Near-zero downtime and data loss, with willingness to pay for it, points to multi-site active-active with near-real-time replication and latency-based routing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pilot light: minutes to hours of recovery.
• Warm standby: faster, but not near-zero.
• Hourly backups: an hour of data loss.

Key takeaway: strictest RTO/RPO → active-active.
Q001091:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB global tables provide multi-Region, multi-active writes with automatic replication.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Aurora Global Database: one writer Region.
• ElastiCache Global Datastore: a cache with one primary.
• RDS Multi-AZ: single Region.

Key takeaway: multi-Region writes → DynamoDB global tables.
Q001093:
Why this is correct:
S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies objects to a bucket in another Region (with Replication Time Control for SLA-backed timing if needed).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same-Region Replication: same Region.
• Nightly CLI sync: manual and delayed.
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds uploads.

Key takeaway: copies in another Region → CRR.
Q001094:
Why this is correct:
A TCP health check passes as long as the port accepts connections, even when the application is failing. An HTTP(S) check on an application endpoint detects the failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alarms on the ASG: unrelated to Route 53 failover.
• Low TTL: helps failover, not detection.
• Manual update needed: failover routing is automatic with health checks.

Key takeaway: health checks must test the application, not just the port.
Q001095:
Why this is correct:
A cross-account role with read-only access to specific buckets and logs, trusted only by the vendor's account (optionally with an external ID), gives temporary, auditable access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root credentials: never.
• Public buckets: exposes data.
• Shared access keys: long-term secrets.

Key takeaway: third-party access → cross-account role (with external ID).
Q001096:
Why this is correct:
Security groups allow the traffic, so the stateless NACL is the likely blocker: it must allow the database port inbound on one side and ephemeral response ports on the other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Missing local route: VPC routes include local traffic automatically.
• Stateless SGs: SGs are stateful.
• Public IP: not needed inside a VPC.

Key takeaway: intra-VPC failures with correct SGs → check NACLs.
Q001098:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB add private routes without NAT and without hourly charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering to S3: not possible.
• Interface endpoints: work but cost more; gateway is the simplest fit.
• NAT gateway: uses the internet path.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB privately → gateway endpoints.
Q001099:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced L3/L4 DDoS protection (and L7 with WAF), while WAF rate-based rules block HTTP floods from abusive sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups: don't absorb DDoS.
• Shield Standard alone: doesn't stop HTTP floods.
• WAF alone: doesn't mitigate network-layer attacks.

Key takeaway: network + application DDoS → Shield Advanced + WAF.
Q001101:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account S3 access needs the bucket owner (Account A) to allow the external principal in a bucket policy, in addition to Account B's identity policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policy in B only: A hasn't granted access.
• Daily copies: duplication and staleness.
• Root user full access: over-privileged.
• Public bucket: insecure.

Key takeaway: cross-account = resource policy + identity policy.
Q001102:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager rotates RDS credentials automatically on a schedule using managed rotation, and applications fetch the current value at runtime, so there's no downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypted config and redeploys: manual.
• Manual console rotation: error-prone.
• Parameter Store SecureString: no built-in rotation.

Key takeaway: automatic DB credential rotation → Secrets Manager.
Q001104:
Why this is correct:
Target tracking keeps average CPU near a target by adding and removing capacity automatically, which suits unpredictable load.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step scaling: more configuration and tuning.
• Scheduled: the load isn't time-based.
• Simple scaling: slower and coarser.

Key takeaway: hold a metric at a target → target tracking.
Q001105:
Why this is correct:
A dead-letter queue receives a message after maxReceiveCount failed receives, removing poison messages so other messages keep flowing and failures can be inspected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual deletion: slow.
• Huge visibility timeout: delays everything.
• FIFO rejecting bad messages: FIFO doesn't validate content.

Key takeaway: poison messages → DLQ.
Q001106:
Why this is correct:
SNS fans out one event to multiple SQS queues, one per consumer, so each system processes independently with its own retries and buffering.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One queue polled by all: each message goes to only one consumer.
• One Lambda calling all: coupled failures.
• Synchronous HTTP calls: tight coupling.

Key takeaway: one event, many independent consumers → SNS to SQS fan-out.
Q001107:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions coordinates Lambda steps with branching, retries, error handling, and visible state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS with manual retries: no workflow state.
• AWS Batch: for batch jobs.
• SNS fan-out: runs everything in parallel without order.

Key takeaway: multi-step workflows → Step Functions.
Q001108:
Why this is correct:
ThrottlingException from DynamoDB and hitting Lambda concurrency limits point to throughput and concurrency limits. Raise quotas or capacity (for example, on-demand mode) and review limits before events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 request limits: not the reported errors.
• ASG max size: Lambda and DynamoDB aren't in an ASG.
• IP exhaustion: shows as ENI errors, not throttling.

Key takeaway: read error names; they point to the limit.
Q001109:
Why this is correct:
A Redis replication group with Multi-AZ and at least one replica fails over automatically to a replica, preserving session data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Memcached: no replication.
• Single node with snapshots: loses data since the last snapshot.
• No replicas: no failover.

Key takeaway: durable Redis sessions → replicas + Multi-AZ.
Q001110:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing sends a chosen percentage of DNS answers to the new version, which can be increased gradually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geolocation: splits by location.
• Simple routing: all or nothing.
• Latency: routes by performance.

Key takeaway: percentage shifts → weighted routing.
Q001111:
Why this is correct:
A termination lifecycle hook pauses termination so the instance can deregister and drain before it's terminated.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grace period: about health checks after launch.
• Termination protection: blocks scale-in entirely.
• Cooldown: timing between scaling actions.

Key takeaway: graceful shutdown in ASGs → lifecycle hooks.
Q001112:
Why this is correct:
If processing takes longer than the visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and another consumer receives it. Increase the timeout to exceed processing time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• FIFO: the queue here is standard.
• Long polling: reduces empty responses; doesn't cause duplicates.
• Exactly-once guarantee: standard queues are at-least-once.

Key takeaway: visibility timeout > processing time.
Q001113:
Why this is correct:
Review Service Quotas usage and request increases for Lambda concurrency and EC2 vCPUs ahead of launch, since increases can take time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More accounts: complexity.
• Request after throttling: failures during launch.
• Spot: may not be available and doesn't remove quota limits.

Key takeaway: plan quotas before demand.
Q001114:
Why this is correct:
Heavy in-memory processing benefits from memory-optimized R instances, with more memory per vCPU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Storage-optimized: for local disk I/O.
• Compute-optimized: less memory per vCPU.
• More general-purpose instances: doesn't fix memory per instance.

Key takeaway: match instance family to the bottleneck.
Q001115:
Why this is correct:
io2 Block Express provides very high, consistent IOPS with sub-millisecond latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp3: tops out at 16,000 IOPS per volume.
• st1 and sc1: HDD for throughput, not IOPS.

Key takeaway: extreme consistent IOPS → io2 Block Express.
Q001116:
Why this is correct:
Lazy loading populates the cache on demand after a miss, so the cache fills with data that's actually requested.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Write-through: fills the cache on writes, including rarely read data.
• Write-behind: delays database writes.
• No cache: doesn't address misses.

Key takeaway: populate on demand → cache-aside.
Q001117:
Why this is correct:
Timestream is a purpose-built time-series database with fast time-range queries and built-in aggregation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Neptune: graph.
• DynamoDB single partition key: hot partitions and no time-series functions.
• QLDB: ledger.

Key takeaway: time-series data → Timestream.
Q001118:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray traces individual requests across services and shows segment latencies, revealing where intermittent slowness occurs that averages hide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More CPU alarms: don't locate slow calls.
• Flow logs and manual correlation: slow and imprecise.
• 1-second metrics: still aggregates.

Key takeaway: find slow hops in distributed systems → tracing.
Q001120:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas use asynchronous replication, so reads may be slightly stale, in exchange for offloading and scaling reads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replicas handle writes: they're read-only.
• Zero lag: not guaranteed.
• More replicas remove lag: they don't.

Key takeaway: read replicas trade freshness for scale.
Q001121:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches video at the edge. Global Accelerator speeds up dynamic, non-cacheable API traffic by routing it over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront for both: works, but Global Accelerator is the purpose-built fit for non-HTTP-cacheable APIs with static IPs.
• Route 53 only: no caching or network acceleration.
• Global Accelerator for video: no caching.

Key takeaway: cacheable → CloudFront; dynamic acceleration → Global Accelerator.
Q001122:
Why this is correct:
High VolumeQueueLength with capped throughput suggests the instance's EBS bandwidth is the limit, for example because it isn't EBS-optimized or its type has limited EBS bandwidth.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Subnet IPs: unrelated to EBS I/O.
• Security groups: don't apply to EBS traffic.
• Placement group: doesn't limit EBS bandwidth.

Key takeaway: EBS performance is also limited by the instance.
Q001123:
Why this is correct:
DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB with microsecond reads and minimal code changes (DynamoDB-compatible API).

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand: capacity mode, not microsecond reads.
• Memcached with custom logic: more work.
• Global Tables: multi-Region replication.

Key takeaway: microsecond DynamoDB reads → DAX.
Q001124:
Why this is correct:
A cluster placement group packs instances close together in one AZ for low latency and high throughput, and enhanced networking (ENA or EFA) boosts it further.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No placement group: less predictable latency.
• Spread: separates instances for resilience.
• Partition: for large distributed stores.

Key takeaway: tightly coupled HPC → cluster placement group.
Q001125:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically based on usage, with no retrieval fees for its automatic tiers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deep Archive for all: slow retrieval.
• Standard-IA for all: retrieval fees for hot objects.
• Fixed 30-day rules: wrong for unpredictable patterns.

Key takeaway: unknown access patterns → Intelligent-Tiering.
Q001126:
Why this is correct:
A gateway endpoint removes S3 traffic from the NAT gateway (no processing charges), and keeping app and database resources in the same AZ reduces cross-AZ transfer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: adds cost.
• Single AZ: sacrifices resilience.
• NAT bandwidth: doesn't change per-GB charges.

Key takeaway: cut transfer costs: endpoints and AZ affinity.
Q001128:
Why this is correct:
A 3-year term gives a bigger discount but locks in spend longer. 1-year is less discounted but more flexible if usage shifts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 1-year bigger discount: the opposite.
• Cancel anytime: not allowed.
• Same discount: longer terms discount more.

Key takeaway: longer commitment = more discount, less flexibility.
Q001129:
Why this is correct:
Aurora or RDS handle patching, backups, and failover, removing DBA toil.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger EC2: same toil.
• S3 as a transactional store: not a relational database.
• More self-managed instances: more toil.

Key takeaway: reduce database operations → managed databases.
Q001131:
Why this is correct:
A stream with too few shards throttles writes from the subscription filter during spikes, so records are delayed or dropped. Add shards or use on-demand capacity mode.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights caching: unrelated to delivery.
• Reserved concurrency requirement: not a requirement.
• kms:Decrypt: would fail consistently, not only during spikes.
• Retention: doesn't delete events before delivery.

Key takeaway: spike-related delivery gaps → downstream capacity.
Q001132:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS runs a replacement task set behind a second target group, switches traffic, and can shift back instantly to the original.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling update: no instant revert to the old task set.
• Manual replacement: slow and error-prone.
• All-at-once with alarms: no instant rollback path.

Key takeaway: instant revert → blue/green.
Q001133:
Why this is correct:
An AWS Fault Injection Service experiment that simulates AZ impairment, with stop conditions, safely tests recovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rule: reports after the fact.
• Manual termination in production hours: uncontrolled.
• Waiting for a real event: no validation.

Key takeaway: test resilience safely → FIS with stop conditions.
Q001134:
Why this is correct:
RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a synchronized staging (green) environment for the upgrade, then switch over with minimal downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snapshot restore and repoint: data diverges and downtime.
• In-place upgrade: no safe testing.
• Replica upgrade and promote: more manual and less controlled.

Key takeaway: safe major upgrades → RDS Blue/Green.
Q001136:
Why this is correct:
Frequent, non-disruptive DRS drills with automated post-launch validation catch configuration problems before a real disaster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only after major releases: drift happens anytime.
• Fewer drills: less confidence.
• Replication metrics alone: don't prove recovery works.

Key takeaway: practice recovery regularly.
Q001137:
Why this is correct:
With a stateful legacy app and an overnight maintenance window, AllAtOnce deploys to every server at once within the window, which is simplest and fastest here.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OneAtATime: may not finish within the window.
• 90% healthy: impractical for this app.
• HalfAtATime: still mixed versions of a stateful app.

Key takeaway: deployment config depends on the app and window.
Q001138:
Why this is correct:
An alarm on a per-InstanceId metric breaks when instances are replaced. Alarm on an aggregate metric (for example, by AutoScalingGroupName or no instance dimension).

Why the other options are wrong:
• More periods: still tied to old instances.
• Missing data as breaching: false alarms.
• Percentile: doesn't fix the dimension.

Key takeaway: alarm on fleet-level metrics for dynamic fleets.
Q001139:
Why this is correct:
Parameter Store SecureString handles thousands of static values cheaply, and Secrets Manager handles the few secrets that need rotation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All in Secrets Manager: costly.
• KMS objects in S3: no parameter management.
• Custom rotation in Parameter Store: reinvents Secrets Manager.

Key takeaway: static config → Parameter Store; rotating secrets → Secrets Manager.
Q001140:
Why this is correct:
Inspector's ECR (enhanced) scanning must be enabled for the repositories. EC2 scanning working doesn't mean ECR scanning is on.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ecr:PutImage: affects pushes, not scanning.
• Inspector can't scan images: it can.
• GuardDuty prerequisite: not required.

Key takeaway: enable scanning per resource type.
Q001141:
Why this is correct:
For singleton stateful instances, Patch Manager in an off-peak maintenance window, followed by application health validation, limits disruption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unattended upgrades: uncontrolled reboots.
• Excluding them: leaves vulnerabilities.
• Monthly replacement: risky for stateful singletons.

Key takeaway: stateful servers need scheduled, validated patching.
Q001142:
Why this is correct:
Organization-wide AWS Backup policies centrally define plans for EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS, with cross-account copies to a vault protected by Vault Lock.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataSync exports: not backups.
• Per-service snapshots: inconsistent.
• 7-day defaults: insufficient.

Key takeaway: central backup governance → Backup policies.
Q001143:
Why this is correct:
An OU-level SCP denying the actions when aws:RequestedRegion isn't an approved Region prevents creation everywhere in the OU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rule: detective.
• Permissions boundaries: per user, easy to miss.
• EventBridge deletion: after the fact.

Key takeaway: prevent Region usage → SCP.
Q001145:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS network to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 latency alone: DNS-level, no network acceleration.
• CloudFront: HTTP(S) content delivery.
• ALB: Regional and HTTP only.

Key takeaway: global TCP/UDP acceleration → Global Accelerator.
Q001146:
Why this is correct:
With EC2 CPU normal, the slowdown likely comes from the database. Performance Insights shows waits, locks, and top SQL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB swap: not the bottleneck.
• More instances: EC2 isn't saturated.
• CloudFront: API responses are dynamic.

Key takeaway: find the bottleneck before scaling.
Q001147:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Keyspaces is a managed, Cassandra-compatible service, removing node tuning and repair.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS PostgreSQL: different data model.
• DynamoDB: requires rewriting for a different API.
• Neptune: graph.

Key takeaway: managed Cassandra → Keyspaces.
Q001149:
Why this is correct:
EMR instance fleets let you specify many instance types and AZs, with On-Demand and Spot targets, maximizing Spot availability and throughput per dollar.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated Hosts: expensive.
• One Spot type in one AZ: interruption-prone.
• RIs for periodic jobs: pays when idle.

Key takeaway: diversified capacity for EMR → instance fleets.
Q001150:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at edge locations with sub-millisecond startup, which is ideal and cheaper for simple header manipulation on every request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Origin-request: changes behavior; runs only on misses.
• Provisioned concurrency: not available for Lambda@Edge.
• More memory: more cost.

Key takeaway: simple, high-volume edge logic → CloudFront Functions.
Q001152:
Why this is correct:
Sustained I/O above the gp3 provisioned IOPS causes the slowdown. Raise gp3 IOPS (up to 16,000) or move to io2 Block Express for more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Size alone: gp3 performance isn't tied to size.
• More instances: a single database.
• S3 for data files: not how PostgreSQL works.

Key takeaway: gp3 performance is provisioned separately.
Q001155:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB Global Tables replicate writes across Regions (typically within a second) in multi-active mode.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering: networking, not replication.
• Custom Streams replication: reinvents Global Tables.
• Backup and restore: not live replication.

Key takeaway: multi-Region active-active DynamoDB → Global Tables.
Q001156:
Why this is correct:
Gateway Load Balancer transparently inserts third-party appliances into the traffic path using GENEVE, with scaling and health checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CLB, ALB, NLB: terminate or route traffic, not transparent inline inspection.

Key takeaway: inline appliances → GWLB.
Q001157:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway in each AZ, with each AZ's private subnets routing to their local one, removes the single-AZ dependency and cross-AZ data charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More bandwidth: still one AZ.
• Consolidate AZs: loses resilience.
• NAT instance: more operations and still single.

Key takeaway: NAT per AZ for resilience.
Q001158:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates continuously, cutting RPO from hours to seconds and enabling fast recovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snowball: offline transfer.
• S3 CRR: objects, not servers.
• AWS Backup: periodic.

Key takeaway: low-RPO server DR → Elastic Disaster Recovery.
Q001160:
Why this is correct:
A circuit breaker stops calling the failing provider, bulkheads isolate its resource use, and queue-based decoupling lets orders be accepted and processed later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Infinite retries: exhaust resources.
• Longer timeouts: tie up threads.
• More instances: still wait on the dependency.

Key takeaway: isolate failing dependencies.
Q001162:
Why this is correct:
A TCP-only health check passes while the application fails. An HTTP(S) check on an application path detects real failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No ALB failover: supported with alias records.
• ALBs can't be checked: they can.
• Low TTL: helps failover, not detection.

Key takeaway: health checks must test what users need.
Q001163:
Why this is correct:
On-demand capacity mode (or auto scaling) adjusts to sudden traffic spikes without manual capacity settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Streams: change capture, not read offloading.
• Lambda concurrency: not DynamoDB capacity.
• GSI: new access pattern, not more capacity.

Key takeaway: spiky DynamoDB traffic → on-demand.
Q001164:
Why this is correct:
A tag policy standardizes the BusinessUnit key, a Config required-tags rule flags untagged resources, and an activated cost allocation tag drives chargeback reports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Untagged filter only: finds gaps too late.
• Manual quarterly audits: slow.
• Self-reporting: unreliable.

Key takeaway: enforce tags to make chargeback accurate.
Q001165:
Why this is correct:
Commit (RIs or Savings Plans) for the steady 10-instance baseline, and use Spot and On-Demand for bursts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RIs for 30: pays for idle peak capacity.
• 100% Spot: risks the baseline.
• 100% On-Demand: overpays.

Key takeaway: commit for the baseline; flexible pricing for bursts.
Q001166:
Why this is correct:
Sustained credit exhaustion means the burstable instance is undersized. A non-burstable or larger class may cost less than paying for surplus credits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RI for t3.medium: locks in the wrong size.
• Downsize: makes it worse.
• Spot for RDS: not available.

Key takeaway: burstable instances suit spiky, not sustained, load.
Q001167:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches content near users, reducing latency and origin data transfer, and its delivery rates are typically lower than S3 direct egress.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replicate to every Region: storage cost.
• Transfer Acceleration: adds cost.
• One Zone-IA: storage class, not delivery.

Key takeaway: global delivery → CloudFront.
Q001168:
Why this is correct:
For a stable workload on one instance family in one Region, EC2 Instance Savings Plans (3-year, all upfront) give the largest discount.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Compute Savings Plans: more flexible, smaller discount.
• On-Demand: no discount.
• 1-year no upfront RIs: smaller discount.

Key takeaway: no flexibility needed → maximize discount.
Q001169:
Why this is correct:
Migration Hub tracks migration status across tools such as Application Migration Service and DMS in one place.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: resource compliance.
• Systems Manager: operations.
• Organizations: account management.

Key takeaway: migration portfolio tracking → Migration Hub.
Q001170:
Why this is correct:
Early waves should be low-risk, low-complexity apps with few dependencies, building momentum and refining the process.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Big bang: highest risk.
• Most critical first: highest risk while the process is immature.
• Alphabetical: ignores risk and dependencies.

Key takeaway: start simple to build the migration factory.
Q001171:
Why this is correct:
Tightly coupled apps should move in the same wave, or keep hybrid connectivity (with acceptable latency) until both have moved.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic reconfiguration: not done by Migration Hub.
• B first regardless: breaks A or adds latency.
• Wait for all discovery: delays unnecessarily.

Key takeaway: plan waves around dependencies.
Q001173:
Why this is correct:
Replatforming keeps the application architecture but swaps a component for a managed service, such as SQL Server on RDS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retire: the app continues.
• Rehost: no component changes.
• Refactor: requires re-architecting code.

Key takeaway: one managed swap, same app → replatform.
Q001174:
Why this is correct:
Negligible usage for 90 days suggests the application isn't needed. Retiring it avoids migration and running costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rehost: pays to move something unused.
• Relocate: same.
• Repurchase: buys a replacement for an unused function.

Key takeaway: don't migrate what you don't need.
Q001175:
Why this is correct:
Relocate with VMware Cloud on AWS keeps VMware tooling and moves VMs quickly without conversion. Rehost with Application Migration Service converts VMs to EC2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Refactor: not needed to keep VMware tooling.
• Identical: they differ in platform.
• Relocate only for Windows: incorrect.

Key takeaway: keep VMware → relocate; go native EC2 → rehost.
Q001176:
Why this is correct:
Migration Evaluator analyzes on-premises utilization and produces a data-driven business case comparing current costs with projected AWS costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer: analyzes existing AWS spend.
• Trusted Advisor: optimizes existing AWS resources.
• Pricing Calculator: manual estimates without on-premises data.

Key takeaway: migration business cases → Migration Evaluator.
Q001177:
Why this is correct:
QuickInsights is a quick view. A detailed assessment adds facilities, licensing, labor, and other on-premises costs, giving a complete comparison.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Assume included: understates on-premises costs.
• Post-migration Cost Explorer: too late for approval.
• Pricing Calculator only: lacks the on-premises side.

Key takeaway: complete TCO needs indirect costs.
Q001178:
Why this is correct:
Migration Hub aggregates tracking data in a single home Region. All teams must use the same home Region to see one consolidated view.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic cross-Region sync: not how it works.
• Delete and recreate jobs: unnecessary if configured correctly.
• Unresolvable: choose one home Region.

Key takeaway: one home Region for Migration Hub.
Q001180:
Why this is correct:
DataSync transfers from NFS to S3 efficiently with incremental syncs, integrity checks, and scheduling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds uploads, not a sync tool.
• Transfer Family: SFTP/FTP endpoints.
• Snowball: offline bulk, not ongoing sync.

Key takeaway: online NFS → S3 with incremental sync → DataSync.
Q001181:
Why this is correct:
At 50 Mbps, 2 PB would take years online. Multiple Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices move data offline within the deadline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Family, Transfer Acceleration, DataSync: all limited by the 50 Mbps uplink.

Key takeaway: do the math on bandwidth; if too slow, ship devices.
Q001182:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Family provides managed SFTP endpoints backed by S3 or EFS, so partners keep using SFTP without a self-managed server.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Direct Connect: private connectivity, not SFTP.
• DataSync: internal transfers, not partner SFTP.
• Transfer Acceleration: HTTP uploads.

Key takeaway: managed SFTP → Transfer Family.
Q001183:
Why this is correct:
S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest edge location over the AWS backbone, speeding long-distance uploads to one bucket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC endpoints: for VPC traffic, not offices.
• CRR: replicates after upload.
• CloudFront: optimized for downloads.

Key takeaway: long-distance uploads to one bucket → Transfer Acceleration.
Q001185:
Why this is correct:
Application Migration Service continuously replicates server volumes at block level, supports test launches, and cuts over with minimal downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DMS full load: databases only, with downtime.
• DataSync nightly copies: not server migration.
• Snowball: offline and slow for cutover.

Key takeaway: rehost servers → MGN.
Q001186:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect gives consistent, high-throughput, low-latency connectivity, and a VPN provides backup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPN primary: variable internet performance.
• Two VPNs: still internet-dependent.
• PrivateLink: not data center connectivity.

Key takeaway: consistent hybrid performance → Direct Connect.
Q001187:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing shifts a growing share of traffic from on-premises to AWS by changing record weights.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: not controlled shifting.
• Multivalue: no control over proportions.
• Geolocation: country-based, not gradual.

Key takeaway: gradual cutover → weighted routing.
Q001188:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center connects to the existing AD, so employees sign in once and receive permission sets across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SAML per account: unmanageable.
• Cognito: for app users.
• Duplicate IAM users: long-term credentials.

Key takeaway: workforce SSO → Identity Center.
Q001189:
Why this is correct:
AD Connector proxies authentication and directory requests to the existing on-premises AD without creating a new directory in AWS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical: they differ.
• Simple AD replicates on-prem AD: it doesn't.
• AD Connector can't serve Windows auth: it can for supported services.

Key takeaway: use existing AD → AD Connector; need AD in AWS → Managed Microsoft AD.
Q001190:
Why this is correct:
DMS full load plus CDC keeps RDS in sync while the source stays live. Cutover only requires a brief stop for the final sync.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snowball export: long downtime.
• DataSync to RDS: can't write RDS data files.
• SCT single export: long downtime.

Key takeaway: minimal downtime → full load + CDC.
Q001191:
Why this is correct:
SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion) converts Oracle schemas and PL/SQL to PostgreSQL and flags items needing manual changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue: ETL.
• DataSync: files.
• DMS: moves data, not code.

Key takeaway: code and schema conversion → SCT.
Q001192:
Why this is correct:
A Control Tower landing zone provides governance, and existing accounts can be enrolled to apply controls consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single account: loses isolation.
• Config without structure: no guardrails.
• Manual SCPs per account: inconsistent.

Key takeaway: govern existing accounts → Control Tower enrollment.
Q001194:
Why this is correct:
Memory pressure on an in-memory analytics app calls for a memory-optimized family such as r6i.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Burstable T: CPU credits, not memory.
• Compute-optimized: less memory.
• CPU-based scaling: doesn't address memory per instance.

Key takeaway: memory-bound → R family.
Q001195:
Why this is correct:
EKS runs upstream-compatible Kubernetes, so existing manifests, Helm charts, operators, and kubectl workflows carry over.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ECS: different API; doesn't accept Kubernetes manifests.
• Lambda: not Kubernetes.
• Beanstalk: not Kubernetes.

Key takeaway: keep Kubernetes investment → EKS.
Q001196:
Why this is correct:
Fargate runs ECS tasks without managing EC2 instances, patching, or cluster scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 with Spot: still manage instances.
• EC2 with manual scaling: more work.
• ECS Anywhere: your own infrastructure.

Key takeaway: no servers to manage for containers → Fargate.
Q001198:
Why this is correct:
EBS volumes persist independently of the instance and provide block storage suited to databases (gp3 or io2 for performance).

Why the other options are wrong:
• EFS: network file system, not the best fit for a database's block storage.
• Instance store: ephemeral.
• S3 mounted: not a block device for databases.

Key takeaway: persistent block storage for DBs → EBS.
Q001199:
Why this is correct:
EFS provides a shared POSIX file system that multiple Linux instances can mount across AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glacier: archive.
• Single EBS on all instances: not supported across AZs and needs a cluster file system.
• Instance store: ephemeral and not shared.

Key takeaway: shared Linux files → EFS.
Q001200:
Why this is correct:
FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB shares with Active Directory integration and NTFS permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3: object storage, not SMB with AD ACLs.
• Volume Gateway: block storage for on-premises.
• EFS: NFS for Linux.

Key takeaway: Windows SMB + AD → FSx for Windows.
Q001201:
Why this is correct:
FSx for NetApp ONTAP keeps NetApp features such as Snapshots and SnapMirror, and Storage Gateway File Gateway serves the second case of on-premises access to S3-backed storage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 for both: no NetApp features.
• EFS and Lustre: no NetApp features.
• Volume Gateway: block storage, not NetApp.

Key takeaway: keep NetApp features → FSx for ONTAP.
Q001202:
Why this is correct:
Simple key-value access at high scale fits DynamoDB, with on-demand or auto scaling for spiky traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed sharded MySQL: heavy operations.
• Large RDS: relational overhead for key-value access.
• PostgreSQL replicas: read scaling, not key-value scale.

Key takeaway: key-value at scale → DynamoDB.
Q001203:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch Service is the managed option for Elasticsearch-style search and log analytics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Kinesis Data Analytics: stream processing.
• PostgreSQL full-text search: limited for log analytics.
• DynamoDB GSI: not full-text search.

Key takeaway: managed search and log analytics → OpenSearch.
Q001204:
Why this is correct:
A third-party engine extension and custom storage engine need OS and database-level control, which self-managed EC2 provides, at the cost of more operations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS Custom: allows OS access, but the option describes it wrongly as allowing no customization.
• Aurora Serverless: no third-party extensions.
• Standard RDS without the extension: breaks the app.

Key takeaway: unsupported engine customizations → self-managed (or RDS Custom where supported).
Q001205:
Why this is correct:
A job that runs briefly each night fits a Lambda function triggered by EventBridge Scheduler (if it fits Lambda's limits), paying only for execution time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ASG with minimum one: still idle cost.
• Bigger instance: idle cost remains.
• RI: discounts an idle instance.

Key takeaway: short scheduled jobs → serverless.
Q001206:
Why this is correct:
Splitting the ETL into steps orchestrated by Step Functions keeps each step within Lambda's 15-minute limit, with retries and state between steps.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More memory: helps speed, but volume keeps growing past 15 minutes.
• Compiled language: temporary relief.
• Reserved concurrency: doesn't extend duration.

Key takeaway: work beyond 15 minutes → decompose and orchestrate.
Q001207:
Why this is correct:
ECS or EKS on Fargate supports long-running tasks with more memory than Lambda, without managing servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlimited Lambda duration: capped at 15 minutes.
• Spot only: Fargate supports long tasks.
• Provisioned concurrency: doesn't remove the timeout.

Key takeaway: long jobs without servers → containers on Fargate.
Q001208:
Why this is correct:
EKS supports Kubernetes-native GitOps tools (such as Argo CD or Flux) with existing Helm charts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Beanstalk: not Kubernetes.
• CodeDeploy: not GitOps for Kubernetes.
• ECS: not Kubernetes.

Key takeaway: Kubernetes GitOps → EKS.
Q001209:
Why this is correct:
Storing attachments in S3 (and sessions in a shared store) removes dependence on any one server's disk, enabling horizontal scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger local disks: still server-bound.
• Nightly sync: stale data.
• Permanent sticky sessions: uneven load and data loss on failure.

Key takeaway: stateless servers scale; move state out.
Q001210:
Why this is correct:
Fargate tasks can mount EFS volumes defined in the task definition, providing shared POSIX storage across tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance store via AMI: Fargate has no AMIs.
• EBS per task: not shared among tasks.
• Glacier as POSIX: not possible.

Key takeaway: shared files for Fargate → EFS.
Q001211:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity down during idle periods, lowering cost for intermittently used environments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-AZ with replicas: expensive for test.
• Global Database: unnecessary.
• Largest provisioned class: wasteful.

Key takeaway: intermittent databases → Aurora Serverless v2.
Q001212:
Why this is correct:
ElastiCache caches frequently read product data in memory, cutting database load and latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More replicas per traffic step: costly.
• OpenSearch replacement: different purpose.
• Global Accelerator: network path, not database load.

Key takeaway: repeated reads → cache.
Q001213:
Why this is correct:
A queue decouples the front end from processing: orders are accepted immediately and processed with retries, so slow services don't block users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More front-end instances: still blocked by slow calls.
• Bigger payment instance: doesn't remove coupling.
• Longer timeouts: worse user experience.

Key takeaway: decouple synchronous chains with queues.
Q001214:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge offers content-based routing rules, a schema registry, and SaaS partner event sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS: no schema registry or SaaS partner sources.
• Step Functions: orchestration, not routing.
• SQS: a queue, not a router.

Key takeaway: event routing across services and SaaS → EventBridge.
Q001269:
Why this is correct:
If the drifted values should be kept, update the template to match them and review a change set before executing; otherwise the next update may revert or fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• continue-update-rollback: for stuck rollbacks.
• Ignore: CloudFormation doesn't auto-reconcile drift.
• Delete and recreate: disruptive.

Key takeaway: resolve drift deliberately through the template.
Q001395:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account AssumeRole needs both the target role's trust policy and an Allow for sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN in the caller's (Lambda execution role's) policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• STS doesn't support cross-account: it does.
• Lambda can't assume other accounts' roles: it can.
• Resource-based policy beyond trust: the trust policy is the role's resource policy.

Key takeaway: AssumeRole needs trust on the target and permission on the caller.
Q001401:
Why this is correct:
SCP-based guardrails prevent actions. Config rule-based guardrails detect and report noncompliance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both preventive: Config rules detect.
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Both detective: SCPs are preventive.

Key takeaway: preventive = SCP; detective = Config.
Q001994:
Why this is correct:
Central Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints in a networking VPC, with private hosted zones associated to the VPCs and forwarding rules shared via RAM, give hybrid DNS for all 60 VPCs without per-VPC endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BIND on EC2 everywhere: heavy operations.
• Endpoints in every VPC: costly and duplicated.
• Public zones: expose internal names.

Key takeaway: centralize hybrid DNS; share rules with RAM.
Q001995:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the inspection VPC's TGW attachment keeps both directions of a flow on the same AZ and appliance, preventing asymmetric routing drops by stateful firewalls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MTU change: unrelated to asymmetry.
• Another AZ endpoint: doesn't fix symmetry.
• Peering everywhere: loses central inspection.

Key takeaway: stateful inspection via TGW → appliance mode.
Q001996:
Why this is correct:
A Deny SCP with a NotAction list exempting global services and a condition on aws:RequestedRegion blocks other Regions without breaking IAM, Organizations, and similar global services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allow-only SCP at root: allow lists don't restrict by themselves unless FullAWSAccess is removed, and globals break.
• Permissions boundaries: per principal, easy to miss.
• Deny ec2/s3 only: other services remain.

Key takeaway: Region restriction = Deny + NotAction for globals.
Q001997:
Why this is correct:
A tag policy defines CostCenter and allowed values (with enforcement), and an SCP denies creation when aws:RequestTag/CostCenter is missing. Together they enforce presence and valid values.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Activate the tag: reporting only.
• Cost Explorer: reporting only.
• Config auto-delete: destructive and after the fact.

Key takeaway: enforce tags at creation: SCP (presence) + tag policy (values).
Q001998:
Why this is correct:
Surviving a device, connection, or location failure requires separate connections on separate devices at two or more Direct Connect locations (the maximum resiliency model).

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX + VPN: VPN has lower bandwidth and different performance.
• Two connections at one location: a location outage takes both down.
• LAG on one device: a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: location-level resilience needs multiple DX locations.
Q001999:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Global Database replicates with typical sub-second lag and supports fast managed failover to the secondary Region, meeting seconds of RPO and minutes of RTO.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Binlog replica with manual promotion: more lag and slower recovery.
• 15-minute backup copies: RPO of 15 minutes.
• Hourly snapshots: RPO of an hour.

Key takeaway: seconds of RPO for Aurora → Global Database.
Q002000:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates continuously to a low-cost staging area and launches recovery instances in minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hourly DataSync: files only, with an hour of RPO.
• Full warm standby: costly.
• Nightly backups: a day of RPO.

Key takeaway: seconds RPO, minutes RTO, low cost → DRS.
Q002001:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS supports a test listener to validate the replacement task set, lifecycle validation hooks, and alarm-based rollback before production traffic shifts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling update: no separate test traffic.
• Restart all at once: no testing or rollback.
• Manual weighted DNS: slow and manual.

Key takeaway: test before shifting → blue/green with a test listener.
Q002002:
Why this is correct:
Multipart upload makes large uploads resilient (retry parts) and parallel, and Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance transfers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CRR: replicates after upload.
• CloudFront GETs: downloads.
• EC2 proxy: a bottleneck.

Key takeaway: large distant uploads → multipart + acceleration.
Q002003:
Why this is correct:
A FIFO queue with the customer ID as the message group ID keeps order per customer while processing different customers in parallel, and deduplication prevents duplicates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard queue: no ordering guarantee.
• Single message group: serializes everything.
• SNS standard: no ordering.

Key takeaway: per-key ordering with parallelism → FIFO message groups.
Q002004:
Why this is correct:
Lambda SnapStart caches an initialized execution environment snapshot for published versions, cutting Java cold starts dramatically without paying for idle capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned concurrency at peak: works but costly for low traffic.
• VPC attachment: adds, not removes, setup.
• Longer timeout: doesn't reduce latency.

Key takeaway: Java cold starts → SnapStart.
Q002005:
Why this is correct:
RDS Proxy pools and reuses database connections, preventing connection storms from bursts of Lambda invocations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More replicas: the writer still gets connections.
• Concurrency 1: throttles the application.
• Bigger writer: raises the limit but doesn't pool.

Key takeaway: Lambda + relational DB → RDS Proxy.
Q002006:
Why this is correct:
Session Manager provides shell access through IAM without open ports or SSH keys, with session logging to S3 or CloudWatch.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rotate keys and restrict port 22: still open ports and keys.
• Bastions: still SSH and extra hosts.
• Instance Connect with port 22 open to the internet: exposure.

Key takeaway: close SSH → Session Manager.
Q002007:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route that traffic privately without NAT processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public subnets: exposure.
• NAT instance: operations, still in the path.
• Interface endpoints: hourly and per-GB costs.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB traffic off the NAT → gateway endpoints.
Q002008:
Why this is correct:
Predictive scaling forecasts the recurring 8 AM increase and launches capacity ahead of time, covering the 7-minute startup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual schedules: need upkeep.
• Longer grace period: doesn't add capacity sooner.
• 10% CPU target: overprovisions all day.

Key takeaway: slow-starting instances + recurring peaks → predictive scaling.
Q002009:
Why this is correct:
Convert the schema (SCT or DMS Schema Conversion), then run DMS full load plus CDC and cut over when lag is near zero, keeping downtime within minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full load only: downtime for the whole copy.
• Data Pump: Oracle format and long downtime.
• Native PostgreSQL logical replication from Oracle: not possible.

Key takeaway: heterogeneous + short downtime → convert + DMS CDC.
Q002010:
Why this is correct:
DataSync copies NFS data to EFS over Direct Connect with incremental tasks, and a final sync at cutover captures the last changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MGN: server replication, not NFS to EFS.
• s3 sync: targets S3, not EFS.
• Transfer Family: SFTP, not NFS migration.

Key takeaway: NFS → EFS migration → DataSync.
Q002011:
Why this is correct:
Application Discovery Service agents collect process-level data and network connections, and Migration Hub shows the dependency maps for wave planning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: AWS accounts only.
• Spreadsheet: no dependencies.
• Agentless only: no process-level data.

Key takeaway: dependencies need agent-based discovery.
Q002012:
Why this is correct:
Application Migration Service replicates VMs continuously until cutover and supports test launches, with minimal changes to the servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DMS: databases.
• VM Import/Export: one-time images without continuous replication.
• DataSync: files.

Key takeaway: rehost at scale → MGN.
Q002013:
Why this is correct:
The strangler fig pattern routes selected paths (for example, with ALB path rules) to new services while the monolith handles the rest, migrating gradually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full rewrite: high risk.
• Cache everything: doesn't modernize.
• Separate URLs: breaks the user experience.

Key takeaway: incremental modernization → strangler fig.
